Stablecoin fees shouldn’t be fixed.

A trade can either push a stablecoin further off-peg or help bring it back.

@Uniswap’s new StablePair Hook treats those two situations differently:

→ Push the pool further off-peg: no fee
→ Help bring it back: the fee starts high and falls until someone takes the trade

Say USDC slips to $0.99 in the pool.

A trader can swap USDT for the cheaper USDC, sell it elsewhere closer to $1, and help push the pool back toward peg.

With the new hook, Uniswap takes a larger cut of that arbitrage profit at first, then lowers the fee until someone takes the trade.

That leaves more profit for LPs.

It's a design change that fixed a real inefficiency.

Sharply lower allocations, fully booked capacity into 2029, and future price hikes doesn't quite sound like the AI buildout is slowing down.

It's easy to psyche yourself out of a good business idea because there’s competition.
 
“Oh someone’s already doing it, it’s too late”
 
1. Competition shows the idea might already be validated

2. Markets can be a lot bigger than you think. nobody wins a whole market anyway. Even the biggest player has like 30%. You don't need to beat them, you need a slice.

3. No one else has your unique experience and judgement. It's like thinking NYC can only support 1 pizza place. There's so many different kinds of pizza.

4. A lot of competitors are stuck in their old ways. Ex some are gonna die bc an A.I. native person's going to be way more efficient.  

I've learned to view competition as a GOOD thing. If 100 people are making money from X, I just have to be better than the guy in 100th place.

That's way easier for me mentally than entering uncharted territory and wondering if the idea's even viable.

Anyways, wanted to write this bc my friend is psych'ing himself out of an idea because he saw there's already competitors.

What the Champions League Can Teach Us About Small-Cap Investing

A good analogy for small-cap investing is soccer.

Imagine a small Israeli team entering the Champions League and trying to beat Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, and the other European giants.

Could it happen once? Of course. Soccer is unpredictable, and occasionally a small team achieves something extraordinary.

But the giants have enormous budgets. They can afford the best players, coaches, analysts, training facilities, and medical teams. The small Israeli team may have talented players and a clever strategy, but over time, the difference in resources becomes almost impossible to overcome.

More importantly, even if one small team eventually succeeds, your chances of predicting in advance exactly which team it will be are close to zero.

The same lesson applies to small caps and microcaps.

Smart Shooter is an Israeli company valued at roughly $300 million. It developed a rifle-mounted fire-control system that helps soldiers identify and track moving targets. The system can also help soldiers hit small drones.

It is a real product and may offer a useful, low-level solution. But investors are taking this limited solution and attaching it to the enormous drone-warfare story. That is how a real product can quickly receive a fantasy valuation.

We saw something similar with $INVZ. The company was supposed to help solve autonomous driving through LiDAR. The dream was enormous, the valuation followed the dream, and shareholders were eventually crushed while the company continued burning cash and raising more capital.

And who used to pump $INVZ ? The now-infamous and convicted Andrew Left, who faces prison after being found guilty of securities fraud.

This is one of the most important questions to ask when investing in a small company:

Does the size of the company match the size of the problem it claims it will solve?

A small biotechnology company may discover a treatment for a rare disease because the opportunity is too small to interest the giants. But when a company claims it will solve one of the largest and most valuable problems in the world, you must consider who it is competing against.

In investing, the Champions League budgets are the R&D budgets.

A small company spending $20 million or $50 million a year on research is competing against companies that can spend $20 billion or $50 billion. The giants have more engineers, more data, more manufacturing capacity, more distribution, greater political access, and far more room to make mistakes.

That does not mean the small company has no useful technology. It means that a useful product and a valuable stock are two completely different things.

During every mania, microcaps attach themselves to the hottest story. Investors stop valuing the business that exists and begin valuing the future they imagine. The stock may rise dramatically while the dream remains popular, but eventually the market asks the only questions that matter:

Where are the revenues? Where are the profits? Where are the resources? And what prevents the giants from taking the market?

Elon Musk managed to challenge the world’s largest automobile companies with Tesla, but he is an extreme exception. You cannot build an investment strategy around finding the next Elon Musk.

Yes, a small company can occasionally defeat the giants, just as a small Israeli team can occasionally beat a soccer team in the Champions League.

But even if it happens once, your chances of correctly predicting beforehand which one will do it are close to zero.

Do not confuse the size of the dream with the probability of achieving it.

Warren Buffett is considered the ultimate fundamental investor, but people misunderstand what made him successful.

Early in his career, Buffett had a genuine information edge. Financial data was difficult to obtain, few investors carefully studied balance sheets, and cheap companies could remain undiscovered for years. Simply reading every annual report and calculating the real value of a business gave him an enormous advantage.

Today, everyone has the same numbers. Every financial statement is instantly available. Thousands of analysts, algorithms, and artificial intelligence systems can compare valuations within seconds. Knowing that a company trades at eight times earnings or below book value is no longer an edge. It is merely information.

This may explain why many investors influenced by Buffett, including Bill Ackman, David Einhorn, and other traditional value investors, have struggled to consistently outperform in recent years. They learned the visible part of Buffett’s process: study the accounts, calculate intrinsic value, and buy when the price appears cheap. But once everybody learned the method, much of its advantage disappeared.

Buffett himself understood this transition. With Charlie Munger’s influence, he moved away from buying statistically cheap but mediocre businesses and toward buying exceptional companies whose future value could not be fully captured by a spreadsheet.

The edge moved from quantity to quality.

The most important questions today are often the ones that cannot be answered precisely with numbers. Is the chief executive changing? Is the culture improving? Do customers genuinely love the product? Is public perception completely disconnected from reality? Is management about to become more disciplined? Has the market misunderstood how people will behave?

These things cannot always be placed neatly into a model, but they matter no less than revenue, margins, and cash flow. In many cases, they matter more because the numbers only describe what has already happened, while qualitative changes determine what happens next.

This is why most investment posts on X are worthless. They repeat numbers, announce that something is cheap, and present publicly available information as analysis. But everyone can see those numbers. Every analyst knows them. Every algorithm has already processed them. Every artificial intelligence system can explain the same apparent valuation within seconds.

Repeating the obvious is not an edge.

The modern investor’s advantage is not having more data. It is understanding what the data cannot yet show. The edge is recognizing a change in human behavior, management, psychology, positioning, or perception before that change appears in the financial statements.

Numbers tell us where the company has been. Qualitative judgment tells us where it may be going.

Such a great story about the impact on communities of a data center created 20 years ago! Re-Industrialization means job creation, new public infrastructure, and thriving small towns! 

« In a time when many rural towns across the country are shrinking, Quincy has grown more than 40 percent, outpacing Seattle. Poverty rates have been cut in half. Over the past two decades, property tax revenue in Grant County has grown twelve-fold, while the rate residents pay has fallen by a third. That revenue has built a new high school, hospital, library and city hall, and it will pay for a future aquatics center.
And at a time when people worry that datacenters bring nothing but a wave of temporary construction jobs, Quincy tells a different story. We've sustained 1,200 construction jobs every year for 20 years by building new datacenters and refurbishing existing ones. We employ close to 700 people on our datacenter campuses in non-construction operational roles. «
